hints: Moving up one parent at a time costs k steps for every query. Any k can be written as a sum of powers of two. What could you precompute to use that?
Use binary lifting. Store up[j][v], the 2j-th ancestor of v, using up[j][v] = up[j-1][ up[j-1][v] ]. For a query, jump once for each set bit of k.

1. up[0] = parent.
  2. For j = 1..LOG: up[j][v] = −1 if up[j−1][v] is −1, else up[j−1][up[j−1][v]].
  3. For a query: for each bit j set in k, set node = up[j][node].
  4. If node becomes −1, return −1.
  5. Return node.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Follow parent k times for each query.

approaches.name: Optimal (binary lifting)
approaches.idea: Precompute 2<sup>j</sup>-th ancestors for every node. Then any k is at most log n jumps.
approaches.time: O(n log n) build, O(log k) per query

explain: With parent = [-1,0,0,1,1,3], we get up[0][5] = 3 and up[1][5] = up[0][3] = 1. For kthAncestor(5, 2), k = 2 has only bit 1 set, so we make one jump of size 2 and return 1. kthAncestor(4, 1) uses up[0][4] = 1. For kthAncestor(2, 3), 3 = 1 + 2: the first jump goes 2 → 0, and the next jump from 0 gives −1, so the answer is −1. The order of the jumps does not matter, because they add up to exactly k levels. Stop as soon as you reach −1 so you never index the array with −1.
recognize: When there are many 'go up k steps' queries on a fixed tree, binary lifting (a table of 2<sup>j</sup> jumps) is the usual tool.
